body:
Why the location of computing matters

Cloud data centres can process very large quantities of information, but sending every piece of information to a distant facility may not always be desirable. Network transmission takes time, uses capacity and depends on the availability of a communication link.

Edge computing is an approach in which some computing and data storage occur closer to the device, user or location that produces the data. The edge may be a sensor-connected controller, a nearby computer, a local gateway or a computing facility situated relatively close to users.

Edge computing does not necessarily replace the cloud. Many systems use edge and cloud computing together.

How edge computing works

Consider a field equipped with soil-moisture sensors and an automated irrigation controller. Sensors generate readings. A nearby controller can examine the measurements and make a time-sensitive decision about irrigation without first sending every reading to a distant cloud service. The system may also periodically send selected information to a cloud application for records, analysis or wider monitoring.

This division of work can be useful when the immediate response matters more than sending all raw readings to a distant server. It also reduces the volume of information that must cross a long-distance network when only selected results need to be transferred.

Benefits of edge computing

  • Lower latency: some decisions can be made without waiting for a distant server to respond.
  • Reduced network traffic: local filtering or processing can reduce the amount of raw data sent across the network.
  • Support during connectivity interruptions: appropriately designed local functions may continue even when the external connection is temporarily unavailable.
  • Local data handling: some information can be processed close to where it is generated, although data protection still requires proper safeguards.

These are potential benefits, not universal guarantees. A poorly designed edge device may still operate slowly, and a service that depends on cloud resources may stop functioning during an internet outage.

Common applications

Traffic management

A roadside computing device can process information from nearby sensors to support local traffic monitoring. Selected summaries can then be sent to a central system. This may reduce the need to send all raw observations continuously.

Industrial monitoring

Equipment sensors in a factory can generate frequent readings. A local computing system can identify basic abnormal conditions and communicate an alert promptly. Longer-term analysis and record keeping may be performed in the cloud.

Healthcare and remote services

A suitable medical monitoring device may process selected readings locally while sending records to authorised healthcare systems when connectivity is available. The safety and suitability of any medical decision depend on the particular approved device and its intended use; edge computing alone does not make a medical system clinically reliable.

Agriculture and rural connectivity

Local processing can help agricultural monitoring systems in areas with intermittent internet connectivity. A field sensor may continue collecting readings locally, with information synchronised when connectivity returns. However, unattended control of physical equipment still needs appropriate safety arrangements.

Edge computing, cloud computing and 5G

5G is a cellular communication technology, cloud computing provides computing resources through a service model, and edge computing places some processing closer to where data is produced or used. A system may combine all 3, but none of the terms is a substitute for the others.

For instance, a 5G link may carry data between a device and a nearby computing facility, while a cloud platform stores historical results. The response time still depends on the whole path, including device processing, radio conditions, network routing and application operation.

Prelims focus

  • Edge computing places some processing near the source or use of data.
  • Cloud computing may still perform central storage and large-scale analysis.
  • Reduced delay and network traffic are possible advantages of edge computing.
  • Edge computing can support locally operating functions during some connectivity interruptions if designed for that purpose.
  • 5G is a communication technology; edge computing concerns the placement of computing work.
  • Trap: Edge computing is not necessarily completely offline, and it does not eliminate the need for cloud services.

[Sources: Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Cloud Native Glossary, 'Edge Computing', definition, problems addressed and examples, consulted 4 November 2026; NIST, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, SP 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, cloud-computing characteristics; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Communications, 'Prime Minister to launch 5G Services in India', 30 September 2022, references to 5G use cases including edge computing.]

title: Edge Computing: Processing Data Closer to Its Source

body:
What makes a digital service reliable?

A useful digital service must do more than transfer data quickly. It must remain available when users need it, protect information appropriately and recover from foreseeable failures. Reliability concerns consistent correct operation, while availability concerns whether the service can be accessed when required.

Failures can occur in a telecommunications link, mobile tower, electricity supply, cloud server, software application or database. A service may also fail because of human error, incorrect configuration or a security incident. Improving one component cannot remove every possible weakness in the complete system.

Resilience through redundancy and recovery

Resilience is the ability of a system to withstand disruption and continue, restore or adapt its operation. Several related measures help improve it.

  • Redundancy: providing more than one suitable component or path so that a single failure need not stop the whole service.
  • Failover: transferring work or traffic to another available component when the normal one fails.
  • Backup: keeping recoverable copies of data so that lost, damaged or incorrectly changed information can be restored.
  • Monitoring: detecting abnormal conditions so that faults can be identified and addressed.
  • Recovery planning: preparing and testing the procedures needed to restore services after disruption.

Why backups and redundancy are not the same

Two active servers may help maintain availability if one fails, but that does not guarantee protection against accidental deletion or corruption. If incorrect data is quickly copied between the servers, both may contain the same error. A suitable backup can preserve an earlier recoverable version.

Likewise, a backup alone may not keep a website continuously available. Restoring data and restarting services can take time. A reliable design therefore considers both continuity of service and recovery of information.

What is vendor lock-in?

Vendor lock-in occurs when changing from one technology or service provider to another becomes difficult or expensive because of dependencies on the original provider.

For example, an organisation may build an application around a particular cloud provider's proprietary database features or specialised software interfaces. Moving the application elsewhere might then require changes to software, data formats, staff skills and operational procedures.

Potential difficulties include:

  • Data portability: difficulty exporting information into usable formats.
  • Application portability: difficulty running the same application in another environment without significant changes.
  • Contractual or financial costs: expenses associated with migration, moving data or ending arrangements.
  • Operational dependence: reliance on tools, skills or services specific to one provider.

Using widely supported formats, maintaining appropriate backups and avoiding unnecessary dependencies can reduce some lock-in risks. Containers may improve application portability, but they cannot automatically remove dependencies on specialised databases, cloud services or external systems.

Moving data out of a cloud is not always the same as moving a working application. Successful migration may also require software changes, suitable security controls, testing and a replacement operating environment.

How the main technologies fit together

Consider an online public-service portal used by people in a rural area. A person may connect through a Wi-Fi hotspot or a cellular network. That access network may carry data over optical-fibre backhaul, while a satellite link may provide connectivity in a location where a terrestrial route is impractical.

The portal itself may run on cloud infrastructure. Its provider may supply virtual resources through IaaS, an application platform through PaaS or a complete hosted application through SaaS. The cloud may be public, private or hybrid according to how the infrastructure is organised.

Some local devices may perform processing through edge computing. The application may use containers for deployment or serverless functions for selected event-driven tasks. Redundant links, reliable authentication, recoverable backups and suitable recovery plans can help the complete service survive disruptions.

Choosing the appropriate technology

There is no single technology that is best in every circumstance. A high-capacity urban backbone may strongly favour optical fibre, while an isolated location may benefit from satellite connectivity. Wi-Fi is useful for local wireless access, whereas cellular infrastructure supports mobility across a wider area.

Similarly, SaaS suits organisations wanting a ready-to-use application, PaaS suits those developing applications without administering the underlying platform, and IaaS suits those needing greater control over the computing environment. Edge computing is valuable where local processing reduces delay or network demand. The choice must reflect the actual requirement, costs, security needs and connectivity conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Radio waves support wireless access; optical fibre carries information as guided light.
  • Wi-Fi is associated with IEEE 802.11, while 5G NR belongs to cellular communication.
  • IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are service models; public, private and hybrid are deployment models.
  • Containers package applications; serverless reduces direct infrastructure-management work; edge computing places some processing near data sources.
  • Redundancy supports continuity, while backups support recovery of data.
  • Trap: More network paths do not replace backups, and using containers does not eliminate vendor lock-in.

[Sources: NIST, The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing, SP 800-145, September 2011, sec. 2, service and deployment models; NIST, 'Cloud Computing' project overview, updated 14 September 2026, consulted 4 November 2026; NIST, Application Container Security Guide, SP 800-190, September 2017, abstract; Cloud Native Computing Foundation, Cloud Native Glossary, 'Edge Computing' and 'Serverless', consulted 4 November 2026; Department of Telecommunications, Digital Bharat Nidhi, Amended BharatNet Programme overview, consulted 4 November 2026.]
